title: Area Agencies on Aging: Home Repair and Modification Help
meta_description: Your local Area Agency on Aging can fund or arrange grab bars, ramps and repairs for adults 60+ through the Older Americans Act. How to call and what to ask.
short: The local Area Agency on Aging is the best first call for adults 60 and older; many fund small repairs and safety changes or know who does.
pays_for: Grab bars, handrails and stair rails
Raised toilet seats, shower chairs and hand-held showers
Small ramps and minor accessibility changes
Minor home repairs that fix safety problems
Caregiver supports such as respite, training and, in some areas, limited supplemental services
Referrals to weatherization, Medicaid waivers, nonprofits and city or county repair programs
who_qualifies: Older Americans Act services are generally for people 60 and older
Many local home modification programs focus on older adults with low incomes, and some also serve rural older adults, veterans and caregivers
Family caregivers of people 60+ (or of people with Alzheimer's at any age) can get help through the National Family Caregiver Support Program
Each local agency sets its own priorities and service list
how_to_apply: Find your local Area Agency on Aging through the Eldercare Locator at eldercare.acl.gov or by calling 1-800-677-1116.
Call and say you are looking for home modification or home repair help for someone 60 or older.
Ask whether the agency provides the work itself, pays a contractor, or refers you to another program.
Ask about waitlists, income priorities, any cost-sharing, and what paperwork they need.
If you are a caregiver, also ask about the Family Caregiver Support Program.
Write down the name of the person you spoke with and any program names they mention.
watch_out: Funds are limited. Many agencies use the same pot of Title III-B money for rides, legal help and in-home care, so repair budgets can run out.
Waitlists are common. Get on the list early.
Services and limits vary a great deal by county. A neighbor's experience in another county may not apply to you.
Some programs only do minor fixes. Larger projects usually need to be combined with other funding.
If someone claims to be 'from the Area Agency on Aging' and asks for payment up front, call the agency directly to confirm.

faq.q: What is an Area Agency on Aging?
faq.a: It is a local agency, often part of county government or a nonprofit, that plans and delivers Older Americans Act services such as meals, in-home help and caregiver support for older adults in a region.

faq.q: Does the Area Agency on Aging pay for home modifications?
faq.a: Many do. A national survey found 61% of responding agencies provide or contract for home modifications and repairs, and others refer people to programs that pay. ACL says your local agency can check whether you qualify for Title III home modification and repair funds.

faq.q: Do I have to be low income?
faq.a: Older Americans Act home modification and repair funds are for people 60 and older. In a national survey, 78% of agency home modification programs served older adults with low incomes, so income often affects priority. Ask your agency how they decide.

faq.q: How do I find my local agency?
faq.a: Use the Eldercare Locator at eldercare.acl.gov or call 1-800-677-1116.

faq.q: Can the agency help me as a caregiver?
faq.a: Yes. The National Family Caregiver Support Program, funded under Title III-E, offers information, help getting services, counseling and training, respite, and limited supplemental services.

body_md:
## Why this is the first call to make

If you are 60 or older, or caring for someone who is, your local Area Agency on Aging (often called the "Triple A") is the best place to start. These agencies run services funded by the Older Americans Act. They know which local programs have money right now, and many pay for home repairs and safety changes themselves.

ACL, the federal agency that oversees them, says it plainly: if you are 60 or older, your local Area Agency on Aging can check whether you qualify for home modification and repair funds under Title III of the Older Americans Act [1].

## What Area Agencies on Aging do

Area Agencies on Aging plan and offer services so older adults can stay in their own homes. Examples include home-delivered meals and homemaker help [2]. Home repair and modification is another common service.

A national survey of Area Agencies on Aging, run by the National Association of Area Agencies on Aging (n4a) and the Scripps Gerontology Center, found [4]:

- 61 percent provide home modifications and repairs, either directly or through local contractors
- Of those, 94 percent do minor changes, 56 percent do repairs, and 52 percent do major changes
- 46 percent refer people to other local home modification or repair programs
- 45 percent refer people to direct funding sources

## Where the money comes from

The main source is Title III-B of the Older Americans Act, known as Supportive Services. In the n4a survey, 67 percent of agencies with home modification programs used Title III-B funds [4].

There is a catch. Agencies also use Title III-B money for rides, legal help and in-home care. That limits how much is left for home changes [4]. This is why waitlists are common and why many agencies also use donations, grants and cost sharing [4].

### Title III-E: help for family caregivers

The National Family Caregiver Support Program, under Title III-E, helps family members and other unpaid caregivers. It covers caregivers of people 60 and older, and caregivers of people of any age with Alzheimer's disease or a related disorder [3].

It offers five types of help [3]:

1. Information about services
2. Help getting those services
3. Counseling, support groups and caregiver training
4. Respite care, which gives caregivers a break
5. Supplemental services, on a limited basis

Whether supplemental services can include safety items depends on your local program. It is worth asking.

## What kinds of home changes are common

ACL lists many changes that help people stay home safely [1]:

- Entry ramps and grab bars
- Walk-in or roll-in showers
- Lever-style door and sink handles
- Better lighting and night lights
- Handrails and wider doorways
- Stair chair lifts
- Medical alert systems

Agency-funded programs usually focus on the lower-cost items on this list. Bigger projects often need help from more than one source.

## The referral network

Even when an agency cannot pay, it can point you to who can. Among agencies that refer people to funding sources, the n4a survey found they most often send people to [4]:

- The Weatherization Assistance Program (88 percent)
- Nonprofits such as Habitat for Humanity or Rebuilding Together (62 percent)
- City or county housing and community development offices (62 percent)
- Medicaid home and community-based services waivers (59 percent)

## How to reach your agency

Use the Eldercare Locator at eldercare.acl.gov or call 1-800-677-1116 [1]. Give your ZIP code and ask for the Area Agency on Aging that serves you.

### What to say on the call

"I am calling about home safety changes for my mother, who is 78. She has trouble getting in and out of the tub. Do you have a home modification or repair program, or can you tell me who does?"

### Questions worth asking

- Do you do the work, pay a contractor, or refer me elsewhere?
- Is there a waitlist? How long is it right now?
- Do you give priority based on income, age or health?
- Is there any cost to us?
- What paperwork do you need?
- Can someone visit the home to see what is needed?
- Do you have help for caregivers?

## Before you call: a quick checklist

Having a few facts ready makes the first call faster and helps staff match you to the right program:

- The older adult's age, address and household size
- A rough idea of monthly household income
- Whether the person owns or rents the home
- The top one or two problems, described in plain words ("can't step over the tub," "front steps have no railing")
- Any recent falls, hospital stays or new diagnoses
- Whether the person is a Veteran or already gets Medicaid, since that can open other doors

If you are a family member calling from out of town, say so. Ask whether the agency can mail or email forms, and whether the older adult needs to be on the call to give permission.

## Tips for renters

If you rent, talk with your landlord before making changes. ACL notes that landlords must allow reasonable modifications for people with disabilities [1]. Your agency can help with questions about this.

## What to expect

Help from an Area Agency on Aging is often quick for small items, like a grab bar or railing. Larger projects take longer and may need several funding sources. Think of the agency as a guide as well as a funder. Their referrals can save you weeks of calls.

Hands-on demonstrations to compare options
Low-cost reused equipment, such as wheelchairs, walkers and shower chairs

faq.q: What is a State Assistive Technology program?
faq.a: It is a program in each state, funded through ACL under the Assistive Technology Act, that helps people find, try and get assistive devices through demonstrations, short-term loans, reuse and financing.

faq.q: Can I borrow a device before buying it?
faq.a: Yes. Short-term device loans are a core service. You can borrow an item for a limited time to see if it works for you.

faq.q: Do they help with home modifications?
faq.a: Some do. For example, Nebraska's AT program has managed ramps, stair lifts, roll-in showers and grab bars. Other states focus only on devices. Ask your state program.

faq.q: Is there an age limit?
faq.a: No. State AT programs serve people with disabilities of all ages, including older adults.

faq.q: How do AT loans work?
faq.a: Many states run alternative financing programs, such as low-interest loans or loan guarantees, to help people buy equipment. Terms vary by state.

body_md:
## A free place to try before you buy

Before you spend hundreds or thousands of dollars on a lift chair, shower bench or ramp, there is a better first step. Every state has a State Assistive Technology program. It helps people find, try and get the right equipment.

There are 56 of these programs: one in each state, Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico and four U.S. territories [1]. They are funded through the federal Administration for Community Living under the Assistive Technology Act.

## What "assistive technology" means

Assistive technology, or AT, is any item or system that helps a person do things more easily or safely. It can be low-tech, like a spoon with a built-up handle. It can also be high-tech, like a home automation system [1].

For aging in place, AT often includes:

- Shower chairs, transfer benches and hand-held showers
- Grab bars and portable rails
- Walkers, rollators and wheelchairs
- Portable ramps
- Lift chairs and stair lifts
- Large-button phones, amplified phones and video doorbells
- Medication reminders and smart-home controls

AT also includes services like assessment, set-up, repair and training [1].

## What State AT programs offer

Most programs offer four main services [1]:

### 1. Device demonstrations

Staff show you different devices side by side and explain the features. This helps you compare before you choose.

### 2. Short-term device loans

You can borrow a device for a while to see if it works in your home. This is one of the most useful services for older adults. A bath bench that looks good in a catalog may not fit your tub.

### 3. Reuse programs

Programs collect used equipment that someone no longer needs and pass it on, often at big savings [1]. This can be a good source for walkers, wheelchairs, shower chairs and more.

### 4. State financing

Some programs offer loans or other ways to buy AT for less, or even at no cost [1]. Federal guidance lists options such as low-interest loans, interest buy-downs, revolving loan funds and loan guarantees [3]. These financing programs are meant to serve people regardless of disability type, age or income [3].

Programs also offer training, information and referrals [1].

## Examples of home help

Some State AT programs do more than lend devices. At a 2023 federal webinar on housing and home changes, presenters shared real examples [2]:

- **Nebraska's AT program** manages home modifications across the state, including entrance ramps, vertical platform lifts, stair lifts, roll-in showers and grab bars. It uses approved contractors, seeks at least two quotes, and warranties work for one year. The average project cost about $8,500 [2].
- **A California disability organization** runs a lending library that loans portable ramps while permanent changes are planned. It also offers no-cost minor changes like grab bars, transfer poles, portable aluminum ramps and railings [2].

These examples show what is possible. Your state may offer more or less, so ask.

## How to find your state program

The AT3 Center keeps a directory of every State AT program at at3center.net/stateprogram [1]. The CATADA website also has state profiles [1].

## What to say when you call

Describe the problem, not just the product. For example:

- "My father is unsteady getting off the toilet."
- "My mother can't get up our two front steps with her walker."
- "My husband has low vision and keeps missing the bottom stair."

Then ask:

- Can we see options at a demonstration center?
- Can we borrow something to try at home?
- Do you have any used equipment that might work?
- Do you offer loans for bigger purchases?
- Do you know of local programs that pay for home modifications?

## Matching common problems to equipment

It can help to think in terms of the daily task that has become hard. Here are common examples to bring up with your state program:

- **Getting in and out of the tub.** Transfer benches, shower chairs, hand-held showers and grab bars.
- **Getting up from the toilet.** Raised seats, toilet safety frames and grab bars.
- **Climbing front steps.** Portable or modular ramps, sturdy rails, or, for bigger budgets, a platform lift.
- **Moving between floors.** Stair lifts, or setting up a first-floor bedroom.
- **Hearing the phone or doorbell.** Amplified phones and flashing-light alerts.
- **Low vision.** Brighter task lighting, high-contrast tape on stair edges and talking devices.
- **Memory changes.** Medication reminders and simple smart-home controls.

Staff can show you several options for each problem and explain the trade-offs, which is hard to get from a store or a website.

## Tips for families

**Try it in the real space.** Measure doorways, tubs and stairs before borrowing. Bring photos if you visit a demo center.

**Think short term too.** A borrowed portable ramp or shower chair can bridge the gap while you wait for funding for permanent changes.

**Ask about returns.** If a borrowed item works, ask where to buy one and whether the reuse program has a similar model.

**Combine with other help.** State AT programs work well alongside Area Agencies on Aging, Centers for Independent Living and state Medicaid waivers.

meta_description: Centers for Independent Living help people with disabilities, including older adults, plan home changes, find funding, and move home from nursing facilities.
short: Centers for Independent Living are disability-led nonprofits that help with advocacy, housing, assistive technology and finding money for home changes.

Assistive technology information and loans in some areas

Independent living skills training and peer support
Advocacy with landlords, agencies and benefit programs

If someone is in a nursing home and wants to go home, ask about transition services.

faq.q: What is a Center for Independent Living?
faq.a: It is a local, private nonprofit run largely by people with disabilities. It helps people with significant disabilities live independently through information, skills training, peer support, advocacy and transition help.

faq.q: Can older adults use a CIL?
faq.a: Yes, if they have a significant disability. Centers are cross-disability, so age-related vision, hearing or mobility loss can qualify.

faq.q: Do CILs pay for ramps or bathroom changes?
faq.a: Housing help and modifications are listed by ACL as services some centers provide. But federal independent living grants cannot be used for home repair, so centers often use other funds or partner with nonprofits and local governments.

faq.q: What is transition help?
faq.a: It is a core CIL service that helps people move from a nursing home or other institution back to the community, and helps people at risk of entering one stay home.

faq.q: Do CILs charge for services?
faq.a: Ask your center directly. Policies can differ from center to center and by service, especially for programs paid for with non-federal funds.

body_md:
## Disability-led help close to home

A Center for Independent Living, or CIL, is a local nonprofit that helps people with disabilities live on their own terms. What makes CILs different is who runs them. People with disabilities hold most of the leadership roles.

According to ACL, about two-thirds of CIL staff are people with disabilities, and they hold 75 percent of decision-making positions [1]. Under federal rules, more than half of a center's board must be people with significant disabilities [3].

There are more than 350 CILs across every state and territory [1].

## Who can use a CIL

CILs serve people with significant disabilities who live in their service area [2]. They are "cross-disability," which means services cannot depend on having one specific kind of disability [3].

This matters for older adults. Many people develop a disability later in life: vision loss, hearing loss, arthritis, a stroke or trouble walking. A CIL can help, whether you were born with a disability or developed one at 75.

## What CILs do

Every CIL offers a set of core services [1]:

- **Information and referral.** Help finding programs and services.
- **Independent living skills training.** Such as managing personal care, budgets and a household.
- **Peer counseling and support.** Talking with someone who has lived with a disability.
- **Advocacy.** For you as an individual, and for wider changes in the community.
- **Transition support.** Help moving from a nursing home or other institution into the community, help staying out of one, and help for young adults leaving school.

Many CILs also offer extra services based on local need. ACL lists examples such as housing searches, home modifications and housing help, assistive technology, transportation, health care navigation and benefits enrollment [1].

## Can a CIL pay for home modifications?

This is where it helps to know the rules.

Some CILs help with home modifications. ACL lists housing modifications among the extra services centers may offer [1]. But federal independent living grant funds cannot be used for "home repair and disaster clean up" [2]. CILs often partner with local governments and nonprofits for this type of work [2].

So a CIL may:

- Run a modification program paid for with other grants or local funds
- Partner with a nonprofit or city program that does the work
- Help you apply to Medicaid waivers, state programs or VA
- Lend portable equipment while you wait

At a 2023 federal webinar, one California disability organization described a "Fix It" program offering no-cost grab bars, transfer poles, portable ramps and railings, plus a lending library for ramps while permanent changes are planned [4]. Not every center has this. But it shows what some do.

## Transition help: going home from a nursing facility

One of the most valuable CIL services for older adults is transition help. If a parent is in a nursing home after a fall or illness and wants to go home, a CIL can help plan the move [1]. That can include:

- Finding out what home changes are needed
- Connecting with Medicaid waiver programs
- Getting equipment in place
- Setting up in-home help

The same service can help someone at risk of going into a nursing home stay home instead [2].

## How to find your CIL

Use ACL's "Find a CIL Near You" tool at dial.acl.gov [1]. ACL also keeps a list of centers by state.

## Getting the most from a CIL

### Go in with a clear picture

Write down what is hard now. "Can't get into the shower." "Can't use the front steps." "Can't reach the kitchen shelves." Specifics help staff point you in the right direction.

### Expect to be part of the plan

CILs are built on the idea that people with disabilities direct their own lives. Staff will work with you, not just for you. Bring the person who needs the help into the conversation whenever possible.

### Ask about partners

Ask: "Who do you work with for ramps and bathroom changes? What funding do people in this county usually use?" CIL staff often know the local system better than anyone.

## What a first contact often looks like

Every center works a little differently, but a first contact usually covers a few basics. Staff will ask where you live, what is hard right now, and what you want to change. They may ask about your income and benefits, since that affects which outside programs you can use.

From there, a staff member may help you set goals, such as "shower safely without help" or "get to the car on my own." They may connect you to equipment loans, help you apply to other programs, or refer you to a partner that does construction. If the person needing help is in a hospital or nursing facility, say so right away, since transition planning works best when it starts before discharge.

## How CILs fit with other help

CILs work well alongside Area Agencies on Aging, which focus on people 60 and older, and State Assistive Technology programs, which lend and finance equipment. For larger construction costs, look at Medicaid waivers, state housing agency programs, USDA repair grants in rural areas, VA grants for Veterans, and nonprofit repair groups.

title: VA Home Modification Grants (SAH, SHA, TRA and HISA)
meta_description: How VA's SAH, SHA, TRA and HISA grants pay for ramps, roll-in showers and wider doors for Veterans with disabilities, with FY2026 maximums and how to apply.
short: Four VA grants that help Veterans with qualifying disabilities adapt a home, from small HISA jobs to whole-house SAH projects.
pays_for: Permanent entrance ramps and wider entry paths
Roll-in showers and accessible bathrooms
Lowered kitchen or bathroom sinks and counters
Wider doorways and hallways
Plumbing or electrical work needed for home medical equipment
Building or buying a new adapted home (SAH)
Adapting a family member's home where the Veteran lives for now (TRA)
who_qualifies: SAH: Veterans or service members who own or will own the home and have a qualifying severe disability, such as loss or loss of use of more than one limb, blindness in both eyes (20/200 or less), certain severe burns, or certain post-9/11 lower-limb losses
SHA: Veterans or service members (or a family member) who own or will own the home, with loss or loss of use of both hands, certain severe burns, or certain breathing injuries
TRA: Veterans who qualify for SAH or SHA and live for a while in a family member's home
HISA: Veterans with a medical need for a home change, prescribed by a VA doctor; the amount depends on whether the disability is service-connected
how_to_apply: Decide which grant fits: large structural projects usually point to SAH or SHA; smaller medically needed changes usually point to HISA.
For SAH, SHA or TRA, apply online through VA's disability housing grants page using VA Form 26-4555, or apply by mail or in person.
For HISA, ask your VA doctor for a prescription that describes the project and the medical reason for it.
Fill out and sign VA Form 10-0103 for HISA. Ask for an advance payment on the form if you need one.
Get a written, itemized contractor estimate covering labor, materials, permits and inspections, and take a color photo of the area before work starts.
If you rent, get a signed, notarized letter from the owner allowing the work.
Do not start work until VA approves it. VA may inspect the home.
watch_out: Starting construction before approval can leave you paying the full bill yourself.
HISA does not pay for porch lifts, stair glides, removable or portable ramps, hot tubs, decks, security systems or routine repairs like a new roof or furnace.
SAH and SHA can be used up to six times over your lifetime, so plan big projects so you do not waste a use on a small job.
Only 120 people per fiscal year can qualify under the single lower-limb SAH category; if the cap is hit you may be able to get the grant in a later year.
VA's fiscal year starts October 1. Amounts can change each year, so confirm the current maximum on VA's page before you plan your budget.
Be wary of anyone who charges a fee to 'get you approved.' Applying to VA is free.

faq.q: How much is the VA SAH grant in 2026?
faq.a: For fiscal year 2026 (which began October 1, 2025), the SAH maximum is $126,526. The SHA maximum is $25,349. VA adjusts these each fiscal year based on construction costs, so check VA's housing grants page for the latest figure.

faq.q: Can I get both HISA and an SAH or SHA grant?
faq.a: They are separate programs run by different parts of VA. HISA comes through VA health care (Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service), while SAH and SHA come through VA housing benefits. Ask both offices how the grants fit your project before you apply.

faq.q: Does a Veteran have to own the home?
faq.a: For SAH and SHA, you (or for SHA, a family member) must own or plan to own the home. TRA covers a family member's home you live in for now. HISA can help renters if the owner signs a notarized approval.

faq.q: Is HISA a one-time payment?
faq.a: No. HISA is a lifetime amount, either $6,800 or $2,000 depending on your disability status. You can use it across more than one project until it runs out.

faq.q: Does HISA pay for a stair lift?
faq.a: VA's HISA page lists stair glides and porch lifts as not covered by HISA. Ask your VA prosthetics office whether the item can be provided another way.

body_md:
## What these grants are

The Department of Veterans Affairs runs four grants that help pay for home changes. Each one has its own rules. Picking the right one first saves months.

- **SAH (Specially Adapted Housing)** is the largest. It can help build, buy or remodel a home for Veterans with the most severe disabilities.
- **SHA (Special Housing Adaptation)** is smaller. It helps adapt a home for certain other serious disabilities.
- **TRA (Temporary Residence Adaptation)** helps adapt a family member's home where a Veteran lives for a while.
- **HISA (Home Improvements and Structural Alterations)** is run by VA health care. It pays for smaller, medically needed changes.

## How much money is available

For fiscal year 2026, which began October 1, 2025, VA published these limits in the Federal Register [2]:

- SAH: up to $126,526
- SHA: up to $25,349 (VA's website shows $25,350)
- TRA for someone who qualifies for SAH: up to $50,961
- TRA for someone who qualifies for SHA: up to $9,099

VA says the maximums can change each year based on construction costs [1]. VA's fiscal year 2027 started October 1, 2026, so check VA's page for any newer figure before you plan.

You can use SAH or SHA money up to six times over your life. You can use some now and save the rest. If the maximum goes up later, your total can rise to the newer cap for the year you last use it [1].

HISA works differently. It is a lifetime amount: $6,800 if the change is for a service-connected disability, or if you have a service-connected rating of at least 50 percent. Everyone else who qualifies can get up to $2,000 [3].

## Who qualifies for SAH and SHA

SAH is for Veterans and service members who own, or will own, the home and have a severe disability. VA's list includes loss or loss of use of more than one limb, blindness in both eyes with 20/200 vision or worse, certain severe burns, and loss or loss of use of a lower leg along with certain other conditions [1].

There is also a category for loss of use of one leg after September 11, 2001, when it makes walking or balancing hard without help. Only 120 people can qualify this way each fiscal year. If you qualify but the cap is reached, you may get it in a later year [1].

SHA covers loss or loss of use of both hands, certain severe burns, and certain breathing injuries. The Veteran or a family member must own, or will own, the home [1].

TRA is for Veterans who qualify for SAH or SHA and are living for a while in a relative's home. You do not need to own that home [1].

## What HISA pays for

HISA is meant for changes your VA doctor says you need for medical reasons. VA lists work like [3]:

- Getting in and out of the home, including permanent ramps
- Roll-in showers and other key bathroom changes
- Lowered sinks and counters in the kitchen or bathroom
- Plumbing or electrical work for home medical equipment

HISA does **not** cover walkways to sheds or garages, hot tubs, decks, new construction, security systems, portable ramps, porch lifts, stair glides, or routine upkeep like a new roof, furnace or air conditioner [3].

## How to apply

### For SAH, SHA or TRA

Apply online through VA's disability housing grants page with VA Form 26-4555. You can also apply by mail or in person [1]. A VA housing agent will review the home and your plans.

### For HISA

You will need a packet with five parts [3]:

1. A prescription from a VA doctor with your contact details, a description of the project and the medical reason
2. VA Form 10-0103, signed (you can ask for an advance payment on this form)
3. If you rent, a signed and notarized letter from the owner
4. A written, itemized estimate for labor, materials, permits and inspections
5. A color photo of the area before work starts

Send it to the Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service at your VA medical center. VA may inspect the site [3].

## Tips from the planning side

**Start with the doctor or therapist.** For HISA, the prescription drives everything. Ask the VA doctor or occupational therapist to describe the exact change, not just "bathroom remodel."

**Get the estimate in writing.** VA asks for an itemized bid. Vague bids slow approval.

**Do not start early.** If a contractor begins before VA says yes, you may end up paying. Wait for written approval.

**Think about the six uses.** Because SAH and SHA can only be drawn six times, bundle small jobs together when you can.

**Watch for fees.** Applying for these grants is free. Be careful with anyone who wants money to "speed up" your VA approval.

## Where this fits with other help

VA grants are often the biggest single source of money for a Veteran's home changes. They can still leave gaps. If a project costs more than your grant, look at your state's programs, local nonprofit repair groups, and the tax rules for medical home improvements covered elsewhere on this site.

body_md:
## The short version

The USDA Section 504 Home Repair program helps homeowners in rural areas fix their homes. It has two parts [1]:

- **Loans** of up to $40,000 at a fixed 1 percent interest rate, paid back over 20 years
- **Grants** of up to $10,000 for homeowners 62 and older, used to remove health and safety hazards

You can combine a loan and a grant for up to $50,000 in total [1]. In areas hit by a presidentially declared disaster, the grant limit is $15,000 [2].

For many older adults in small towns, this is one of the best deals around. A 1 percent rate is far below what most banks charge.

## Who can use it

You must own the home and live in it [1]. You must also be unable to get affordable credit somewhere else.

### The rural rule

The home must be in an area USDA counts as rural. This is not the same as "country." Many small towns and some areas near cities still qualify. USDA has an Income and Property Eligibility website where you type in an address and get an answer [2].

### The income rule

Your household income must be at or below the "very low" income limit for your county [1]. USDA defines very low income as 50 percent of the area median income [3]. Because the limit is based on local incomes, the dollar amount changes a lot from county to county. Check the USDA eligibility site for your county's number.

### The age rule

Grants are only for homeowners who are 62 or older [1]. Loans do not have an age rule.

## What the money can pay for

**Loans** can be used to repair, improve or update a home, or to remove health and safety hazards [1].

**Grants** can only be used to remove health and safety hazards [1].

What does that mean for aging in place? Hazards often include:

- Steps or a porch that are unsafe to climb
- A bathroom where an older person is likely to fall
- Broken railings or loose flooring
- A failing furnace in a cold climate
- Unsafe wiring or plumbing

Projects like ramps, grab bars or a safer shower may qualify as hazard removal when they protect an older or disabled resident. Your local USDA office makes the call, so describe the safety risk clearly when you apply.

## How the loan and grant mix works

If you are 62 or older, USDA looks at how much you can afford to pay each month. If you cannot afford any payment, you may get a grant only. If you can afford some payment, you may get part loan and part grant. If you can afford the whole cost as a loan, you may get a loan only.

This is why it helps to be honest and complete about your income and bills. A clear picture can lead to a better mix.

## How to apply, step by step

1. **Check your address.** Use the USDA Income and Property Eligibility site [2].
2. **Check your income.** Look up the very-low-income limit for your county on the same site.
3. **Call your local Rural Development office.** Ask if you can prequalify. It is encouraged but not required [1].
4. **Fill out the forms.** USDA lists forms including RD 410-4, RD 3550-1 and RD 3550-4, plus a checklist [1].
5. **Get estimates.** Have a contractor write up the work and cost.
6. **Wait for approval.** Do not let anyone start before you have it in writing.

USDA takes applications all year while funds last, and processes them in the order they come in [2].

## Things to know before you sign

**Selling soon? Think twice.** If you sell the home within three years, you must repay the grant [1].

**Bigger loans take longer.** Loans over $25,000 need full title service [2]. That can add paperwork and time.

**Money can run out.** Funds are first come, first served. Applying early in the federal fiscal year, which starts October 1, can help.

**Grants are lifetime.** The $10,000 grant limit is a lifetime cap, not per year [1]. Use it for the most important safety fix first.

## Questions to ask the USDA office

- Is my address eligible?
- What is the very-low-income limit for my household size here?
- Will the grant cover my specific safety project?
- Do you have funds left this fiscal year?
- How long are approvals taking right now?

## How it fits with other help

Section 504 often pairs well with other programs. The Weatherization Assistance Program may cover insulation and furnace work, while 504 handles the safety repairs. Local nonprofits and Area Agencies on Aging can sometimes fill small gaps. Veterans should also look at VA grants.

body_md:
## Why Medicaid matters for home changes

Many families think of Medicaid only as nursing home coverage. But every state also uses Medicaid to pay for care at home. These are called home and community-based services, or HCBS.

Many HCBS programs can pay for home modifications. That can include ramps, grab bars, safer showers and wider doors. The idea is simple: changing a home often costs less than a nursing home.

## What an HCBS waiver is

Most of this help comes through "1915(c) waivers." Under these, states design programs that pay for long-term care at home for people who would otherwise need an institution [1]. Nearly every state and Washington, D.C. offers them [1].

Each waiver serves a set group. Common groups include older adults and people with physical disabilities [1]. Waiver services must cost no more than institutional care and follow a person-centered care plan [1].

States may cover a long list of services. These often include case management, personal care, homemaker help, adult day care and respite [1]. States can add other services that help people stay out of institutions.

Home modifications are common. A KFF survey found that 47 states cover "equipment, technology, and modifications" in at least one home care program [2].

### The names vary

Your state may not use the word "waiver" in public. Programs have state names. The home change service might be called "environmental accessibility adaptations," "environmental modifications" or "home accessibility." When you call, use all of these terms.

## Who qualifies

You must meet three kinds of rules.

### 1. Medical or functional need

You must need the level of care that would qualify you for a nursing home or other institution under your state's rules [1]. In practice, this usually means needing help with daily activities like bathing, dressing or eating [2]. A nurse or care manager will do an assessment.

### 2. Financial rules

Rules differ by state. KFF reports that most states allow income up to 300 percent of the SSI benefit and usually limit assets to $2,000 per person [2].

In 2026, the federal SSI benefit is $994 a month for one person [4]. Three times that is about $2,982 a month. If your state uses the 300 percent rule, that is roughly the income ceiling. Check with your state, since some use other limits.

If you are married, states can use "spousal impoverishment" rules [1]. These protect some income and assets for the spouse who is not applying.

### 3. Target group and openings

You must fit the waiver's target group. And the waiver must have room. States choose the most people each waiver can serve [1]. When it is full, new applicants wait.

## About waiting lists

Waiting lists are real and worth planning around. In 2025, KFF found:

- 41 states had waiting or interest lists for waiver services [3]
- More than 600,000 people were on these lists nationally [3]
- Older adults and people with physical disabilities made up about 23 percent of people waiting [3]
- For that group, the average wait was 15 months [3]

Some states screen people before adding them to a list. Others do not, so some people on lists may not qualify [3]. Either way, it pays to apply early.

## How to apply

1. **Find the right door.** Call your state Medicaid agency, your Area Agency on Aging, or an Aging and Disability Resource Center. Ask which waivers serve older adults.
2. **Ask the key question.** "Does this waiver cover home modifications, and what is the dollar limit?"
3. **Apply for Medicaid.** If you are not already on Medicaid, you will need to apply.
4. **Do the assessment.** A nurse or care manager will check your level of care.
5. **Get on the list.** If there is a waitlist, join it now.
6. **Build the care plan.** Once enrolled, work with your care manager to add the home change. Most states require approval and bids before work starts.

## Tips for families

**Document the need.** A letter from a doctor or occupational therapist that explains fall risk or mobility limits can help.

**Ask about the cap.** Most waivers limit how much they spend on home changes per year or over a lifetime. Plan the most important fix first.

**Talk to an elder law attorney before moving money.** Giving away assets to qualify can cause a penalty period.

**Use the time on the waitlist.** While you wait, ask about other help, such as Area Agency on Aging funds, USDA repair grants in rural areas, or local nonprofits.

## How this fits with other programs

Medicaid waivers are often the strongest option for someone who already needs a lot of daily help and has limited income. For people who do not yet need nursing-home-level care, look at Older Americans Act services, state housing programs and nonprofit repair groups instead.

body_md:
## The honest answer

Original Medicare does not pay for remodeling. It will not cover a contractor to build a ramp, widen a door or turn a tub into a walk-in shower.

What Medicare does cover is medical equipment used at home, plus some in-home care. And some Medicare Advantage plans now offer extra benefits that can help with safety items or even larger changes.

This guide sorts out what is covered, what is not, and how to check your own plan.

## What Original Medicare covers

### Durable medical equipment

Medicare Part B covers "durable medical equipment" when a doctor orders it and it is medically necessary for use in your home [1]. Examples on Medicare's list include canes, walkers, wheelchairs and scooters, commode chairs, hospital beds and oxygen equipment [1]. Medicare's equipment booklet also lists patient lifts that move you from a bed or wheelchair [2].

These items can make a big difference in daily safety. A bedside commode can prevent nighttime falls. A hospital bed can make getting up easier.

**Your cost:** After the Part B deductible, which is $283 in 2026, you generally pay 20 percent of the Medicare-approved amount [5]. That is only true if the supplier is enrolled in Medicare and accepts assignment. A supplier that does not accept assignment can charge more [1].

### Home health care

If you are homebound and need part-time skilled care, Medicare covers home health services. That includes physical and occupational therapy when you meet the conditions [3]. You pay nothing for covered home health services [3].

An occupational therapist visiting your home will often point out fall risks and suggest changes. That advice is valuable, even though Medicare will not pay for the changes themselves.

### What Original Medicare leaves out

Medicare's own list of things it does not cover includes non-medical long-term care [6]. Home health benefits do not include 24-hour care, homemaker help unrelated to your care plan, or custodial care when that is your only need [3].

Bathroom safety items like grab bars and shower seats are not on Medicare's covered equipment list [1].

## What Medicare Advantage plans may cover

Medicare Advantage plans are run by private companies. They must cover what Original Medicare covers, and many add "supplemental benefits." Two kinds matter for home safety.

### Home and bathroom safety devices

In 2018, CMS told plans they could offer home and bathroom safety devices as a supplemental benefit [4]. CMS examples include:

- Shower stools and hand-held showers
- Bathroom and stair rails
- Grab bars
- Raised toilet seats
- Temporary or portable ramps
- Night lights and stair treads

Plans may also pay for installation and a home safety check by a qualified health professional [4]. Plans can set who qualifies, such as members at risk of falls.

Under this benefit, CMS does **not** allow structural changes. Permanent ramps, wider halls or doorways, and easy-use doorknobs and faucets were all listed as not allowed [4].

### Special benefits for the chronically ill

A separate category, called Special Supplemental Benefits for the Chronically Ill (SSBCI), gives plans more room. In 2019 guidance, CMS said these benefits can include structural home changes, such as wider hallways or doorways, permanent ramps, and easy-use doorknobs and faucets, when they are expected to help the member's health or function [7].

To qualify, a member must meet all three CMS tests [7]:

1. Have one or more serious chronic conditions that are life-threatening or greatly limit health or function
2. Be at high risk of hospital stays or other bad outcomes
3. Need intensive care coordination

Only some plans offer SSBCI home changes. Those that do must check and document who qualifies [7].

## How to find out what your plan covers

1. **Read your Evidence of Coverage.** Search it for "safety," "bathroom," "home modification" and "chronically ill."
2. **Call member services.** Ask: "Do you cover home and bathroom safety devices? Is there a dollar limit? Do you cover installation? Do you offer special benefits for the chronically ill that include home modifications?"
3. **Get answers in writing.** Ask the plan to send a written summary or point to the page in your plan documents.
4. **Shop during open enrollment.** If these benefits matter to you, compare plans each fall. Benefits can change from year to year.

## A smart order of steps

Start with your doctor. Ask about equipment that Medicare covers and whether home health is right for you. Let the therapist do a home safety review.

Then check your Medicare Advantage plan, if you have one, for safety benefits.

For bigger projects, look beyond Medicare. Your Area Agency on Aging, state Medicaid waiver programs, USDA repair grants in rural areas, VA grants for Veterans, and local nonprofits are where the real remodeling money usually comes from.

## Beware of "Medicare will pay" sales pitches

Some ads and callers claim Medicare will cover a walk-in tub or stair lift. Original Medicare does not cover these. If someone says your plan will pay, call the number on your plan card and confirm it yourself before you sign anything.

body_md:
## What CDBG is

The Community Development Block Grant program, or CDBG, is federal money that HUD sends to cities, counties and states each year. Local governments decide how to spend it within federal rules.

Many communities use part of their CDBG money for home repair programs. Some of those programs focus on older homeowners and people with disabilities. That makes CDBG one of the most common sources of local home repair grants in the country.

## Who gets the money

### Larger cities and counties

Cities that are the main city of a metro area, other cities with at least 50,000 people, and urban counties with at least 200,000 people get CDBG money straight from HUD. These are called "entitlement" communities [2].

### Smaller towns and rural areas

Cities under 50,000 and counties under 200,000 usually get CDBG money through their state. 49 states and Puerto Rico run a State CDBG program. Hawaii does not, so HUD runs it there for the smaller counties [3]. Each state sets its own priorities and decides how to share out the money [3].

## You cannot apply to HUD

HUD does not give CDBG help directly to people. Residents need to contact their city or county officials, who run the program and choose projects [1]. If local officials cannot help, the HUD field office for your area can point you in the right direction [1].

## What CDBG can pay for

CDBG can fund rehabilitation of homes [1]. Federal rules also make "improvements designed to remove material and architectural barriers" that limit access for elderly or severely disabled people an eligible rehab cost [4].

In practice, local CDBG home programs often cover:

- Ramps and entry changes
- Bathroom accessibility changes
- Roofs, furnaces, water heaters and plumbing
- Electrical safety repairs
- Code violations and health hazards

Rules allow the help to come as grants, loans, loan guarantees, interest supplements or other means [4]. Your local program chooses which.

## Who qualifies

### The income rule

At least 70 percent of each community's CDBG money must benefit low- and moderate-income people over a one- to three-year period [2].

For a single-family home, the household living in it must be low- or moderate-income [6]. HUD has made clear that for barrier removal in a private single-unit home, the household's income must qualify. Age or disability alone does not count [5]. HUD measures this against its lower-income limits for your area and household size [5]. Your local program will tell you the dollar amount.

### Other common local rules

Local programs often add their own rules, such as:

- You must own and live in the home
- Property taxes and mortgage must be current
- The home must be insured
- Priority for older adults, people with disabilities or emergency repairs

## How to find your local program

1. **Search your city or county website.** Try "housing rehabilitation," "home repair grant," "minor home repair" or "community development."
2. **Call the housing or community development office.** Ask, "Do you have a home repair or accessibility program for homeowners?"
3. **In a small town, call your county.** Ask whether the county or a regional council has a State CDBG housing grant.
4. **Ask your Area Agency on Aging.** In a national survey, 62 percent of agencies that refer people to funding sent them to local city or county housing and community development offices [7].

## What the process looks like

Most programs follow a similar path:

1. Application and income check
2. Home inspection
3. A written list of work, often prepared by program staff
4. Contractor bids, usually managed by the program
5. Signing grant or loan papers
6. Work, inspections and sign-off

From application to finished work can take months. Emergency repair programs may move faster.

## Documents to gather now

Local CDBG programs ask for proof before they can spend federal money. Having these ready can move you up the line:

- Recent income proof for everyone in the household, such as Social Security award letters, pension statements and bank statements
- The deed or another proof that you own the home
- Your latest property tax bill and homeowner's insurance page
- A photo ID
- Any letter from a doctor or therapist about mobility or fall risk
- Photos of the problem areas

## Read the fine print

**Is it really a grant?** Many programs use deferred or forgivable loans. You may owe money back if you sell, refinance or move out within a set number of years.

**Is there a lien?** Some programs record a lien on the home until the terms are met.

**What is the cap?** Ask how much the program can spend per home. If the cap is low, plan the most important safety fix first.

**What happens if you pass away?** Ask how heirs are treated under the loan terms.

## How CDBG fits with other help

CDBG programs are often the backbone of city and county home repair efforts. They pair well with weatherization for energy work, Area Agency on Aging funds for small safety items, and nonprofit volunteer repairs. If you live in a rural area, also check USDA Section 504 repair grants.

body_md:
## What the HOME program is

HOME Investment Partnerships, usually just called HOME, is a federal block grant from HUD. HUD calls it the largest federal block grant to state and local governments aimed only at creating affordable housing for low-income households [1].

HUD sends HOME money to states and to cities and counties called "participating jurisdictions." They often work with local nonprofits [1]. Smaller towns may get HOME help through their state or by joining a group of local governments.

Local programs can use HOME to build, buy or fix up affordable housing, help with rent, and more [1]. For older homeowners, the most useful part is homeowner rehabilitation.

## How HOME helps homeowners

Many states and cities run "owner-occupied rehab" programs with HOME money. These programs fix up homes owned by lower-income households.

HUD's guidance on homeowner rehab lists accessibility for disabled persons as an eligible cost [3]. That can include changes like ramps, bathroom changes and wider doors, as part of a rehab project.

Help can come in different forms. The most common are grants, deferred-payment loans, no-interest loans and interest-bearing loans [3].

## Who qualifies

### Income

Your household's income must be at or below 80 percent of the area median income [2]. Programs check income before giving help, based on what the household expects to earn over the next 12 months [3]. HUD publishes the dollar limits for each area and household size, and your local program can tell you yours.

### Ownership and living in the home

You must own the home, and it must be your principal residence [2][3].

### Home value

After the work is done, the home's value cannot be more than 95 percent of the median purchase price for your area [2][3]. This rarely blocks modest homes, but it can matter in pricier areas.

## What a HOME rehab is like

HOME rehab programs usually look at the whole house, not just one problem. HUD guidance says a program focused only on accessibility is allowed only if the home meets, or will be brought up to, HOME property standards [3]. So if you ask for a ramp, the program may also need to fix a bad roof or unsafe wiring.

That can be a good thing. You may get more work done. But it also means:

- A full home inspection
- A detailed list of work
- Bids and contracts handled by the program
- Inspections during and after the work
- More time from start to finish

## The affordability rules

Programs that use HOME must protect the public investment. For homeowners, that usually means a loan or agreement that lasts a certain number of years. If you sell or stop living in the home during that time, you may have to repay some or all of the help [2]. The exact rules depend on your local program.

Read these terms closely and ask:

- Is this a grant or a loan?
- Is it forgiven over time? How many years?
- Will a lien be placed on the home?
- What happens if I need to move to assisted living?
- What happens when I pass away?

## How to find a HOME rehab program

1. **Call your city or county housing department.** Ask, "Do you have an owner-occupied rehabilitation program?"
2. **Call your state housing finance agency or state housing department.** Many states run HOME rehab programs for smaller towns.
3. **Ask your Area Agency on Aging or a Center for Independent Living.** They often know which local programs are open.

## HOME versus CDBG

Both programs are run by local governments with HUD money. HOME is only for affordable housing [1]. CDBG can be used for a wider range of community projects. Many cities blend both into one home repair program, so you may not even know which one paid for your work.

## Getting ready to apply

Programs that use federal money must document everything. You can speed things up by gathering:

- Income proof for every adult in the home, such as Social Security letters, pension and retirement statements, and recent bank statements
- Proof that you own the home and live there, like the deed and a utility bill
- Your homeowner's insurance and property tax records
- A list of problems in the home, with photos
- Any doctor or therapist notes about why accessibility changes are needed

If an adult child is helping, ask the program what permission forms are needed so they can talk with staff for you.

## Tips for older homeowners

**Be patient but persistent.** Waitlists are common. Ask where you are on the list every few months.

**Keep your paperwork current.** Income documents may need to be updated if the wait is long.

**Ask about emergency repairs.** Some programs have a faster track for urgent safety problems.

**Plan for the long term.** If you might move in a few years, understand the repayment rules before you sign.

body_md:
## Why it matters for aging in place

Staying home safely is not only about grab bars and ramps. A drafty house, a broken furnace or a carbon monoxide leak can be just as dangerous for an older adult. High energy bills can also squeeze a fixed income.

The Weatherization Assistance Program, run by the U.S. Department of Energy, tackles these problems for free. It is delivered by nearly 700 local providers and weatherizes an average of about 35,000 homes a year with DOE funds [4].

## What it does

A trained auditor visits the home, tests it, and recommends work based on its heating and cooling needs [5]. Typical work includes [5]:

- Insulating the attic, walls and floors
- Insulating the water heater and exposed pipes
- Sealing air leaks with weatherstripping and caulk
- Replacing broken glass
- Tuning up, repairing or replacing the furnace or air conditioner
- Installing ventilation fans

The program also aims to remove energy-related hazards, such as carbon monoxide from a faulty furnace [4]. After the work, an inspector checks it [5].

On average, DOE estimates weatherized households save $372 a year on energy, in 2022 dollars [4].

## Who qualifies

### Income

The federal limit is 200 percent of the poverty guidelines [2]. States may choose to use a rule based on the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), but it must be at least as generous [2]. The exact dollar limit depends on household size and is updated every year, so check with your state office.

Households that received certain cash assistance in the past 12 months, such as SSI, can qualify without a separate income check [2][5].

### Who gets priority

Federal rules list these priority groups [3]:

- Elderly persons
- Persons with disabilities
- Families with children
- High energy users (optional for states)
- Households with a high energy burden (optional for states)

If you or someone in your home is older or has a disability, say so when you apply.

### Renters and home types

Both homeowners and renters can apply. That includes single-family homes, apartments and mobile homes [5]. Renters need written permission from the landlord before work starts [5].

## How to apply

DOE's advice is simple: find your state weatherization administrator and reach out [1]. DOE's website has a map with links to each state [1]. From there:

1. **Find your local provider.** Your state office will point you to the agency serving your county, often a community action agency or local government [5].
2. **Apply.** You will need proof of income for everyone in the home [5]. Recent utility bills are also helpful.
3. **Get on the schedule.** There may be a waitlist.
4. **Have the audit done.** Plan to be home for a few hours.
5. **Let the crew work.** Most jobs take a few days.

## Getting ready for the audit

The energy audit is the heart of the program. A little preparation helps it go smoothly:

- **Clear a path** to the attic hatch, basement, crawl space, furnace and water heater.
- **Gather a year of utility bills** if you can. They help show how much energy the home uses.
- **Make a list of problems** you notice, such as cold rooms, drafts, frost on windows or a furnace that cycles on and off.
- **Mention health concerns.** Tell the auditor if anyone in the home uses oxygen, has breathing problems or is sensitive to cold or heat.
- **Plan for pets and visitors.** Crews may need to move through every room.

Auditors often use a "blower door" test, which uses a fan to find air leaks. It is noisy but harmless. They also check gas appliances for safety. If an older adult will be home alone, a family member may want to be there to ask questions.

## Common surprises

**The audit decides the work.** Weatherization uses testing and cost-effectiveness rules. You may want new windows, but the audit may call for attic insulation instead.

**Some homes have to wait.** If a home has major problems like a badly leaking roof or serious mold, the agency may hold off until those are fixed. Ask whether they partner with a repair program to solve this.

**Approval can expire.** Eligibility lasts 12 months from certification if work has not started [3].

## What weatherization does not cover

Weatherization is about energy and energy-related safety. It does not pay for grab bars, ramps, walk-in showers or wider doors. For those, look at your Area Agency on Aging, local CDBG or HOME repair programs, USDA Section 504 in rural areas, or nonprofit repair groups.

The good news is that these programs often work together. In a national survey of Area Agencies on Aging, 88 percent of those that refer people to funding sources said they refer to weatherization [6].

## Scam alert

Weatherization is free to eligible households [5]. If someone knocks on your door claiming to be from the "government energy program" and asks for money, close the door and call your state weatherization office.

body_md:
## A program built around work

Every state has a vocational rehabilitation (VR) agency. VR helps people with disabilities prepare for, get and keep jobs [1]. That can include paying for home changes, but only when they help you work.

This guide is for adults who still work, want to go back to work, or are looking for part-time work later in life. If you are fully retired, see the note on older adults who are blind below, and the other programs on this site.

## Who qualifies

The federal test has two parts [1]:

1. You have a physical or mental impairment that is a substantial barrier to getting or keeping a job.
2. You need VR services to reach your job goal and can benefit from them.

There is no age limit in this test. A 64-year-old who had a stroke and wants to return to a part-time job can apply, just like a 30-year-old.

### When there is not enough money

If a state cannot serve every eligible person, it must give priority to people with the most significant disabilities [1]. This is called an "order of selection." It can mean a wait for others.

## How home modifications fit in

Federal law lists "rehabilitation technology" among VR services [3]. Many states use this category to cover home changes when they remove a barrier to work.

South Carolina's VR policy is a clear example of how this works [4]:

- The change must remove a home barrier that blocks employment, and must tie directly to the job goal in the person's approved plan.
- Common areas include ramps and lifts, bathrooms, bedrooms, kitchens, and ways in and out of the home.
- A new room addition is approved only if a rehabilitation engineer documents it as the most cost-effective fix.
- The home must be structurally sound. Owners must not be facing repossession; renters must be in good standing.
- Renters need written permission from the owner before work begins.
- A financial need review may set the person's share of the cost.
- Work contracted before VR approval is the person's cost.

Other states have their own versions of these rules. Ask your counselor for your state's written policy.

## Step by step

### 1. Find your agency

The Rehabilitation Services Administration lists all state VR agencies. There are 78 in total. In 22 states, one agency serves people who are blind or have low vision and another serves everyone else. The rest have one combined agency [2].

### 2. Apply

You will fill out an application and meet a counselor. Bring medical records and anything that shows how your disability affects work.

### 3. Build your plan

You and your counselor will write an Individualized Plan for Employment, or IPE. It names your job goal and the services you need.

### 4. Connect the home barrier to the job

This is the key step. Be specific. "I can't get my wheelchair down the front steps, so I can't get to the bus for work." "I can't get into the shower, so I can't get ready for my job each morning."

### 5. Assessment and bids

Expect a home assessment by rehabilitation technology staff and contractor quotes. Do not start work before approval.

## Real-life examples of a work link

These examples show the kind of connection a counselor looks for. They are illustrations, not promises of what any state will approve.

- **A bookkeeper with multiple sclerosis** now uses a wheelchair and cannot get down three front steps to reach her ride to work. A ramp directly removes the barrier to her job.
- **A part-time retail worker recovering from a stroke** cannot safely use his tub to get ready each morning. A roll-in shower may be linked to his return-to-work goal.
- **A self-employed consultant** works from home but cannot get from the bedroom to her home office upstairs. A change that gives her access to her workspace may be tied to keeping her business going.

In each case, the person can clearly explain how the home change affects the job. That is what moves a request forward.

## For adults 55 and older who are blind or have low vision

There is a separate program that does not require a job goal. Independent Living Services for Older Individuals Who Are Blind serves people 55 and older with severe vision loss [5]. It helps with:

- Daily living skills like cooking, housekeeping and grooming
- Orientation and mobility, which means getting around safely
- Training on assistive technology

Contact your state's VR agency for the blind, or the combined agency, to ask about it.

## Tips

**Lead with the job.** VR is not a home repair program. Frame every request around your work goal.

**Get it in the plan.** If a home change is not in your IPE, it is unlikely to be paid for.

**Keep copies.** Save your plan, approvals and quotes.

**Use other help too.** If VR covers part of a project, programs like Medicaid waivers, state housing agencies or nonprofit repair groups may help with the rest.

## Why nonprofits are worth a call

Government programs often have long waits and strict rules. Nonprofit repair groups can be faster and more flexible. They use volunteers, donations and grants to fix homes for people who could not afford the work otherwise.

Two national networks are the best known: Rebuilding Together and Habitat for Humanity. Many towns also have local "minor home repair" or "handy helper" groups run by churches, senior centers or community agencies.

## Rebuilding Together

Rebuilding Together has more than 100 local affiliates in 38 states and Washington, D.C. [1]. Most of the people it helps are veterans, people with disabilities, older adults or families with children [1].

### Who qualifies

Household income typically must be at or below 80 percent of the local area median income [1]. Each affiliate sets its own rules [1]. Most help homeowners, and some help renters [1].

### What they do

Rebuilding Together lists work such as [1]:

- Bathroom changes like grab bars
- Wheelchair ramps
- Roof repairs
- Heating and cooling repairs
- Window and door replacement
- Mold removal
- Painting and yard work
- Smoke alarm installation

### A local example

One Virginia affiliate runs a quick-repair program built around about 40 common fixes, such as grab bars, double stair rails, comfort-height toilets and brighter lighting [4]. Jobs take about half a day with a $500 materials budget, and repairs are free to the homeowner [4]. Priority goes to older adults, people with disabilities, families with children and veterans [4].

Not every affiliate works this way, but it shows how much a short visit can do.

## Habitat for Humanity

Many people know Habitat for building new homes. Many Habitat affiliates also help current homeowners age in place.

### Who qualifies

Local affiliates set their own age and income rules. In general, Habitat works with low-income homeowners in their early to mid-60s or older [2].

### What they do

Inside the home, Habitat aging-in-place work can include safety bars, better lighting, floor repairs, an ADA-compliant toilet and sink, walk-in showers, and energy-efficient doors and windows [2]. Outside, it can include entry ramps, roofs, siding, paint and porch repairs [2]. Some affiliates do only interior or only exterior work [2].

Affiliates may also connect homeowners with partners for meals, groceries and rides to the doctor [2].

### The CAPABLE model

Some Habitat affiliates use CAPABLE, a program developed at the Johns Hopkins School of Nursing. It combines occupational and physical therapy with home repairs and changes [2]. Habitat reports that one study found an average savings of $22,120 per participant over 24 months, and a 30 percent drop in depressive symptoms [3].

## How to find help near you

1. **Rebuilding Together:** Use the "Find Your Local Affiliate" map on rebuildingtogether.org [1].
2. **Habitat for Humanity:** Search for your local affiliate on habitat.org and ask about aging-in-place or home repair services [2].
3. **Your Area Agency on Aging:** In a national survey, 62 percent of agencies that refer people to funding sent them to nonprofits like Habitat or Rebuilding Together [6]. Your agency may know smaller local groups too.

## How to make a strong request

Nonprofits often have more requests than they can fill. A clear, complete request helps.

- **Describe safety first.** "My mother fell getting out of the tub last month" is more useful than "we want a new bathroom."
- **Be specific.** List the two or three most important fixes.
- **Share photos.** Pictures of steps, the bathroom and any damage help staff plan.
- **Have paperwork ready.** Proof of income, ownership and insurance are commonly requested.
- **Be flexible on timing.** Volunteer programs may schedule work around build days or events.
- **Stay in touch.** If your situation changes, like a new fall or hospital stay, let the group know.

## Questions to ask

- Do you serve my town or county?
- What is your income limit for my household size?
- Do you help renters?
- Is there any cost to me?
- Do you have a waitlist or an application season?
- Do you do bathroom changes, ramps, or both?

## Avoiding fake "charity" repair offers

Scammers sometimes pose as charity crews or say they have leftover materials from a nearby job. The Federal Trade Commission warns about contractors who knock on your door, pressure you to decide now, or ask for full or cash-only payment up front [5].

Protect yourself:

- Contact the nonprofit using the phone number on its official website.
- Never pay in full up front.
- Do not sign anything with blank spaces.
- Ask a family member or trusted friend to review any contract [5].

## Combining nonprofit help with other programs

Nonprofits are great for small and medium safety projects. They also fill gaps, like a ramp while you wait for a larger government grant. For bigger jobs, combine their help with city or county repair programs, USDA Section 504 in rural areas, VA grants for Veterans, or Medicaid waivers.

body_md:
## When a reverse mortgage makes sense for home changes

For many older homeowners, the house is their biggest asset. A reverse mortgage lets you turn some of that value into cash without selling or making monthly mortgage payments. That cash can pay for a walk-in shower, a ramp, a stair lift or even a first-floor bedroom.

It is also expensive and complicated. This guide explains how the most common type works, what it costs, and when it may not be the right fit.

## What a HECM is

The most common reverse mortgage is the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage, or HECM. It is insured by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) and offered through FHA-approved lenders [3].

You can keep living in the home as long as you keep up with property taxes and homeowner's insurance [3]. HUD says money from a HECM can be used for home maintenance, repairs or living expenses [3].

## Who can get one

According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau [2]:

- You must be 62 or older.
- The home must be your main residence, where you live most of the year.
- You must own the home outright or have a small enough mortgage to pay off at closing. The reverse mortgage can be used to pay it off.
- You cannot owe federal debt, like federal income taxes or federal student loans. Loan money can be used to pay it off.
- The home must meet the lender's property standards. If not, the lender will list repairs needed before approval.
- You must meet with a HUD-approved reverse mortgage counselor.

## How much you can get

For FHA case numbers assigned on or after January 1, 2026, the HECM maximum claim amount is $1,249,125 nationwide [1]. That is a ceiling on the home value used in the math, not the amount you get.

The amount you can actually borrow depends on [3]:

- The age of the youngest borrower or eligible non-borrowing spouse
- Current interest rates
- The lowest of the appraised value, the FHA limit, or the sale price

Older borrowers and lower interest rates generally mean more money.

## What it costs

A HECM has real costs. The biggest are:

- **FHA mortgage insurance.** Rates set in 2017 are 2 percent of the maximum claim amount upfront and 0.5 percent of the loan balance each year [5]. Ask your lender to confirm current rates.
- **Interest.** Interest is added to the loan each month, so the balance grows [4].
- **Closing costs and fees.** These vary by lender. Compare quotes.

You still pay property taxes, insurance and upkeep [4]. You must either have the money for these or set aside part of the loan at closing [2].

## How you get the money

HECMs offer several ways to take funds. Every option limits how much you can access in the first year [4]. Taking one large lump sum usually gives you less money overall, and you pay interest on funds even if you do not spend them [4].

For home changes, ask your counselor about a line of credit. It can let you draw what you need when the contractor's bill is due, instead of borrowing it all at once.

## When the loan is repaid

The loan comes due when the last borrower or eligible spouse sells the home, moves out or dies [4]. Heirs usually sell the home to pay it back. Neither you nor your heirs will owe more than the home is worth [4].

## Counseling is required, and useful

Before you get a HECM, you must meet with a HUD-approved counselor [2]. Find one through HUD or by calling 800-569-4287 [4]. The CFPB suggests bringing any lender quotes to the session [4]. A good counselor will also talk about other options.

## Questions to ask your counselor and lender

- How much could I get at my age and today's rates?
- What are all the upfront costs, and which can be paid from the loan?
- Which payout option fits a home project that will be paid in stages?
- Will you require repairs before closing? How are they paid?
- How much will I need to set aside for taxes and insurance?
- What happens if my spouse is not on the loan?
- What happens if I move into assisted living for more than a year?

Write the answers down, and compare them across at least two lenders.

## Alternatives to compare

The CFPB suggests looking at other choices first [4], such as:

- Waiting until you are older, when you may qualify for more
- A home equity loan or line of credit
- Refinancing
- State or local property tax deferral or repair help
- Moving to a more affordable home

For home changes specifically, check grants first. Area Agencies on Aging, USDA Section 504, VA grants, Medicaid waivers, state programs and nonprofit repair groups may cover all or part of the cost without a loan.

## Red flags

- A salesperson who pairs a reverse mortgage with a home improvement contract and pushes you to sign quickly
- Pressure to buy an annuity or investment with the loan money
- Anyone discouraging you from talking to a counselor, a lawyer or family

The CFPB's advice: proceed with caution, and do not sign until you understand how the loan works [4].
